title: Chapter 9 – The Deacon's Scale
html:
The Azure Cloud Sect comes for its tribute on the first clear morning after the autumn rains, and it comes by air.

Lin Jian is on the threshing floor behind the storehouse when he feels it: a pressure in the sky, faint and high and moving fast, like the shadow of a hawk passing over a field of mice. He looks up. Everyone on the hill looks up. Out of the west, over the shoulder of the far ridge, a long, slim shape is sliding through the air toward them at the height of a tall pine.

It is a boat. A narrow, graceful hull of pale wood, shaped like a willow leaf, perhaps twenty paces from end to end, with no sail and no oars, gliding over the terraces as smoothly as a skiff on still water. A faint blue haze clings to its keel. As it passes over the gate, the guards in the yard below look up at it with their mouths open, and Old Gou drops his spear.

"Willow-leaf flying boat," says Old Hu, who has come out of the granary to watch with a jar in his hand. "Profound grade. Sect issue. Takes a Foundation cultivator to fly it." He drinks. "Takes three to build it, and a year."

The boat slows over the main courtyard and settles, as gently as a leaf on a pond, until its keel hangs a foot above the flagstones. Two young men in pale blue robes with white cloud emblems on the chest step off its rail, not jumping, simply stepping out onto the air, and drift down to the stones as lightly as falling feathers.

Lin Jian watches their feet. Watches the Qi gather under their heels in two small, spinning cushions. Watches it disperse as they land.

Featherfall, he thinks, and files it away.

Beside him, someone small tugs at his sleeve. Lin Yue is five now, all elbows and sharp eyes and a voice like a startled bird, and she has escaped Old Nan again to come and see. She stares at the two young men standing on the air above the flagstones as though they are gods.

"Brother," she whispers. "Can they fly?"

"The boat flies. They float down."

"Will I float down? When I'm big?"

Lin Jian looks at his sister. At her sealed channels, which he has seen from the inside, perfect and complete and closed like the doors of an empty house. The register in the library says Spiritual root: none in their grandfather's careful hand. Everyone on the hill knows it, and is kind to her about it, the way people are kind to a child who will never walk.

"Yes," he says.

She beams at him and runs off to tell Old Nan, and he stands watching her go, and adds nothing to his list, because the fifth line has been there for five years already.

Then the third passenger steps off the boat, and Lin Jian goes very still.

\ \ \*

Deacon Mo Lian does not look like much.

He is a thin, neat, small man, narrow-faced, with a trimmed mustache and long fingers stained with ink, wearing a pale blue robe with a border of silver clouds. He carries a lacquered case under one arm. He looks like a clerk. He looks, Lin Jian thinks, exactly like the men in his first life who came to the lab once a year with clipboards to count the fire extinguishers.

But the pressure that comes off him is not a clerk's.

It is heavier than the pressure Lin Jian felt on the far ridge from the leader of the wolf pack, a peak-tier beast as heavy as his grandfather. This is denser, with a weight to it that makes the air in the courtyard feel thick. Foundation Establishment. Early, he guesses, from the way it moves, restless and not quite settled, like water that has only just frozen.

And with it, faint and cool and sweeping, something else. A sense. It brushes across the courtyard like a breeze, touching the guards, the servants, the family drawn up on the steps of the main hall. It is idle and careless, the way a man glances around a room. But it is there.

Spiritual sense. A true one, the kind that comes with the Foundation.

Lin Jian steps back behind the corner of the storehouse, out of its path, and lets it go past him. Then he goes into the main hall by the back way, through the kitchen, and slips behind the folding screen in the corner with his eye to the torn third hinge, and stays there for the rest of the day, very small and very quiet, thinking about nothing at all.

He has made one rule for himself about the Sect. He will not scan anything a Foundation cultivator is touching, ever. A Qi Refining cultivator might feel the cold thread of a scan and think it a draft. A Foundation cultivator with a true spiritual sense will feel it and know exactly what it is.

He does not know what the Sect does with a boy who can look inside things. He does not intend to find out.

\ \ \*

The tribute is weighed in the main hall.

Grandfather sits in the Patriarch's chair. The family stands along the walls. Deacon Mo sits at a small table that the servants have set out for him, opens the lacquered case, and takes out a set of brass scales so finely made that they glitter, and a little stack of brass weights, and a jade token that he sets beside the scales and touches once, lightly, with his fingertip.

Before he begins, the deacon takes a small silk pouch from his sleeve, shakes out a single stone, and lays it in the pan of the scale to set the balance.

It is no bigger than the nail of Lin Jian's thumb. But it is not gray-white and faintly glowing, like the stones in the Lin treasury. It is clear as water, with a light inside it like a coal seen through ice, and the moment it touches the brass, the Qi in the whole hall seems to lean toward it.

A mid-grade spirit stone. Lin Jian has read about them. A hundred low-grade stones make one mid-grade, in the markets, and a hundred mid-grade make a high-grade stone, which no one in this county has ever seen. Foundation Establishment cultivators cultivate with mid-grade stones the way his family cultivates with low-grade ones. The Lin treasury, in all its hundred and fifty years, has held perhaps three.

The deacon uses one as a counterweight.

Second Uncle brings the tribute chest. Three hundred low-grade spirit stones, counted out in rows on a cloth.

Deacon Mo weighs them. One at a time.

He holds each stone up to the light. He turns it. He sets it on the scale, and watches the needle, and sets it on one of two cloths at his elbow, the long one or the short one. It takes most of the morning. No one speaks. The only sound in the hall is the click of stone on brass and the occasional sigh of the deacon's breath.

When he is finished, there are two hundred and eighty-nine stones on the long cloth and eleven on the short one.

"Cloudy," says Deacon Mo, touching the short pile. "Cracked. Underweight. Several of them all three." He has a light, dry voice, faintly bored, like a man reading a list of grocery prices. "The Sect accepts only sound stones, Patriarch. You know the rule. Eleven short."

Grandfather says nothing. His face does not change.

Lin Jian, behind the screen, looks at the eleven rejected stones on the short cloth. They look exactly like the others. He knows that is not proof of anything. He has never seen the inside of a stone a Foundation cultivator has just held, because he has never dared to look.

He does not look now, either. Not while the deacon's hand is on them.

\ \ \*

"There is a further matter," says Deacon Mo, and takes a folded document from his sleeve.

He reads it aloud in the same dry voice. The Outer Affairs Hall of the Azure Cloud Sect, it says, has established a new rule for the tributary families of the outer counties. Any family whose trade income has risen by half or more in a single year shall pay a trade levy of one part in five of the increase, to support the Sect's market wardens in their protection of the county roads.

"A new rule," says Grandfather. "This year."

"This year," agrees Deacon Mo. "Proposed by a member of the outer court, I believe. The Outer Affairs Hall found it reasonable."

He does not say which member of the outer court. He does not need to. Everyone in the hall knows which family on Red Ridge has a seat there.

"Our income," says Second Uncle smoothly, stepping forward with his account book, "rose from forty stones to seventy-two, Deacon. An increase of thirty-two. One part in five of thirty-two is six and two-fifths."

"Seventy-two." Deacon Mo looks at him for the first time. "The Sect's market wardens in Willow Ford estimate the Lin shop's income this season at about a hundred and twenty."

The hall goes very quiet.

"The wardens are mistaken," says Second Uncle. His smile does not falter. "They see the boxes go in. They don't see what it costs us to make what's in them. Paper. Ink. Charcoal. Labor. Our margins are much thinner than they look."

Deacon Mo considers him for a long moment. Lin Jian, behind the screen, sees the faint, cool sweep of the deacon's spiritual sense pass over Second Uncle like a hand passing over a table, and sees Second Uncle's smile tighten, very slightly, at the corners.

"Very well," says the deacon. "The Sect asks only what it is owed, and the family's own account is the family's own account." He makes a note. "Seven stones' levy, rounded in the Sect's favor. Eleven short on the tribute. Eighteen owed, Patriarch."

Eighteen stones. After the tribute is paid, the treasury holds forty-one. It can be done. It will leave the family with almost nothing for the winter.

Grandfather opens his mouth.

"Deacon," says Lin Wenyuan quietly, from the wall, "may I offer something else instead?"

\ \ \*

He does not wait for permission. He walks across the hall to the deacon's table with a lacquered box in his hands, and opens it, and sets it down.

Inside, in neat rows, are a hundred Mirror Guard talismans on the new paper, drawn in the new ink, with the lower curl of the ninth character closed last.

"The Sect's Talisman Pavilion buys Mortal-grade talismans from the outer counties," he says. "For its outer disciples, and for the market wardens. I know the price is usually a fifth of a stone for a Mirror Guard. I would ask the Deacon to test one before he names a price for these."

Deacon Mo looks at him. Then at the box. Then he picks up a talisman, holds it to the light as he held the stones, and tears it.

"Guard," he says.

A sphere of gold light blooms over his table, two paces across, so bright that it lights the whole hall. It rings faintly, like a struck bell. One of the outer disciples by the door takes a half step back.

Deacon Mo looks at it. He waits. He counts, Lin Jian can see him counting, his lips moving very slightly under the trimmed mustache. Twenty breaths. Thirty. Forty.

At fifty-two the sphere finally fades.

The deacon sits for a moment in silence, looking at the place where it was.

"A quarter stone each," he says at last.

"The tribute is eighteen."

"A quarter stone each, a hundred talismans. Twenty-five stones." The deacon closes the box. "The Sect takes eighteen in talismans and pays the family seven in coin." He looks up at Lin Wenyuan with something that is not quite a smile. "And the Talisman Pavilion will want two hundred more each season, at the same price, delivered to the market warden in Willow Ford. If you can make them."

"We can make them," says Lin Wenyuan.

Grandfather, in the Patriarch's chair, bows. It is not the formal bow of courtesy that he gives Zhao Heng. It is lower, much lower, and it is directed not at the deacon but at his son.

Lin Jian, behind the screen, does the arithmetic. Two hundred talismans a season at a quarter stone each. Fifty stones a season. Two hundred a year. Two-thirds of the tribute, paid in paper.

It is a lifeline. It is also, he understands, a leash. From now on, the Sect will notice if the Lin talismans stop.

\ \ \*

"And then," says Deacon Mo, "there is the matter of the paper."

He has picked up another talisman and is holding it to the light again, not looking at the characters now, but at the sheet itself. "This is not county paper," he says. "Not even Willow Ford paper. I have seen paper like this in the Sect's own Talisman Pavilion, made by a master with a formation-heated vat. Who made it?"

"I did," says Old Hu, from the back of the hall.

Every head turns.

The deacon looks at the one-armed refiner for a long moment. "Guest Elder Hu," he says. "Of the islands, I'm told. The Talisman Pavilion would be very interested in your method."

"I'm sure it would."

"It would pay well."

"A craftsman's method," says Old Hu, "is his rice bowl, Deacon. If the Pavilion wants the paper, it can buy the paper. If it wants the method, it can hire me." He takes a long drink from his jar. "I'm not for hire."

There is a pause. Then, to Lin Jian's surprise, Deacon Mo laughs: a short, dry, genuine laugh, like a door creaking open.

"Island manners," he says. "Very well. The Pavilion will buy the paper." He closes his case.

Lin Jian lets out a breath he did not know he was holding. Old Hu did not lie. He made the machine. He said nothing else. The wall holds.

\ \ \*

The deacon is packing his scales when one of the outer disciples comes in from the courtyard with a sealed letter.

"From the Zhao family of Red Ridge, Deacon," he says. "Their steward asked that it be read before the Lin family, in the deacon's presence, as the Compact requires."

The deacon breaks the seal and reads it, and his eyebrows rise very slightly.

"A petition," he says. "To the Outer Affairs Hall, through this deacon's office." He reads aloud, in his dry voice: "The Zhao family of Red Ridge respectfully claims the source of the spring on the ridge above the eastern terraces of Green Pine Hill, and the channel that runs from it, as lying within the lands granted to the founder of the Zhao family by survey a hundred and forty years ago. The Zhao family asks that the Outer Affairs Hall appoint an arbiter to settle the matter, in accordance with the Compact, at the arbiter's convenience in the coming spring."

Silence.

The upper channel. Lin Jian knows it the way he knows his own hands. The stone-lined runnel that carries water from a spring on the ridge down to the eastern terraces, where a third of the clan's spirit rice grows. The same water that runs, at the bottom of its long path down the hill, through the runoff channel along the east wall and turns the waterwheel that drives the beater that makes the paper.

Without that channel, the eastern terraces dry out by midsummer. And there is no paper, and no talismans, and no contract with the Talisman Pavilion.

"The founder dug that channel with his own hands," says Grandfather. His voice is very quiet. "A hundred and fifty years ago. Every child on this hill knows it."

"I don't doubt it, Patriarch." Deacon Mo folds the letter. "But that is the kind of thing an arbiter will want to see written down." He tucks the letter into his sleeve. "The Compact does not permit tributary families to settle disputes over land with swords. That is why there are arbiters. The arbiter will come in the spring. He will look at the spring, and the channel, and the deeds and surveys of both families. And he will decide." He picks up his case. "Arbiters," he adds, almost kindly, "do so love records."

\ \ \*

When the flying boat has gone, sliding away westward into the afternoon sky, the family stays in the main hall in silence.

Third Aunt breaks it first.

"A third of the rice," she says. Her voice is tight. "The eastern terraces are a third of our rice and half of my herb beds. If that water stops at midsummer, everything on them is dead by the autumn."

"It won't stop," says Fourth Uncle. He has his arms folded and his jaw set, and Lin Jian has never seen his steady, cheerful uncle look like this. "Let them take the spring to their arbiter. Let them win. Then let one of their stewards come up the ridge and try to dam our channel. I have thirty men who'll stand on that ridge and—"

"And what?" says Grandfather.

Fourth Uncle stops.

"And what, Wenshi?" The old man does not raise his voice. "Your thirty farmers stand on the ridge. The Zhao send their stewards to dam the channel, by the arbiter's ruling. Your farmers push them off. Someone is hurt. Someone, perhaps, is killed." He looks at his youngest son. "And then the Zhao go to the Outer Affairs Hall and say that the Lin Clan has defied a Sect arbiter's ruling and raised its hand against a neighbor under the Compact. And then it is not the Zhao who come up our hill. It is the Sect's Enforcement Hall." He lets that sit. "Do you want to know what the Enforcement Hall does to a tributary family that defies an arbiter? I have seen it once. I was younger than you."

Fourth Uncle looks at the floor.

"Zhao Heng is not a fool," says Grandfather. "He could have sent men to dam that spring at any time in the last forty years. He didn't. He waited until we needed the water for something more than rice. He waited until we had a contract with the Sect that depends on it." He looks around the hall. "He does nothing the Compact forbids. Everything he does is lawful. That is what makes him dangerous."

"Then what do we do?" says Third Aunt.

"We find what the arbiter loves," says Grandfather. "Records."

His eyes rest on his second son as he says it. Second Uncle, by the wall, has his hand on Fourth Uncle's arm, saying something low and earnest about appeals, and about what the Outer Affairs Hall charges a family that loses one. Fourth Uncle is not listening. He is watching his father.

Slowly, the old man's gaze rests on the hand on Wenshi's arm.

Second Uncle's hand slides away.

That night, Lin Jian, lying awake, sees a lamp moving across the courtyard toward the back of the main hall. Toward the library, where the old records are kept, and where Second Uncle keeps his account books on the bottom shelf.

The lamp goes into the library and does not come out again until dawn.

\ \ \*

The next evening, he climbs onto the low wall at the edge of the threshing floor, which is about the height of a grown man, and jumps off it.

He has spent the afternoon thinking about the outer disciples' feet. About the two small spinning cushions of Qi that formed under their heels as they stepped off the rail, and dispersed as they landed. It is a wind art, he is almost sure. Wood and metal again, the same pairing as Cloudstep, but turned downward, spun flat, so that instead of knocking a man's feet out from under him, it catches them.

The first time, he lands on his backside. The second time, on his face. The third time, he manages a faint puff of air under his left foot and none at all under his right, and lands lopsided and turns his ankle, and has to sit on the threshing floor for a while casting the Ward Art on it one element at a time.

On the eleventh jump, as the light is going, he feels it. The wood thread spinning one way and the metal thread the other, a small, tight vortex under each heel, and for one heartbeat he hangs above the stones, not falling, as if the air has turned to water. Then he drops the last half foot and lands, quite softly, on both feet.

He stands very still on the threshing floor, listening to his heart.

Below the storehouse, in the shadow of the eaves, Uncle Mao is leaning on his cane, watching. The old man meets his eyes, and nods once, slowly, and limps away without a word.

The next morning, in the courtyard lesson, Uncle Mao announces that the older children will begin learning Featherfall this autumn, "since our visitors have reminded me that some of you still fall out of trees like sacks of rice," and Lin Jian sits among the others and fails at it, carefully, for a month.

\ \ \*

He has one more thing to do, and he does it two days later.

The eleven rejected stones are back in the treasury chest, waiting to be traded in Willow Ford for something the Sect will accept. No Foundation cultivator has touched them since the tribute. He lifts the lid while Second Uncle is at breakfast and lays his hand on the short row, one stone at a time, and then on a stone from the long row, the accepted ones, beside them.

```
[Comparative Scan: Low-Grade Spirit Stones (11 rejected / 1 accepted)]
Mass: within 0.4% (all)
Clarity: equivalent
Internal fractures: none detected (all)
Energy density: equivalent (±2%)
Conclusion: No meaningful difference between rejected and accepted stones.
```

He closes the lid very quietly.

That afternoon, he finds his grandfather on the eastern wall and tells him, in a child's words: that he looked at the stones the deacon threw out, and they looked the same as the others. That he couldn't see any cracks. That they felt the same.

His grandfather listens without surprise.

"Every deacon does it," he says at last. "Eleven stones. Fifteen. Twenty, in a bad year. Some of it goes to the Outer Affairs Hall. Some of it goes into his own sleeve. Nobody checks." He looks out over the terraces toward the west, where the boat disappeared. "It's what the Compact costs, little builder. The Sect keeps the Zhao from walking up this hill with a sword. In exchange, the Sect takes what it likes, and calls it rules." He is silent a moment. "The Zhao can't kill us. Not while the Compact holds. So they petition. They levy. They claim our water. They do everything the Compact allows, and they do it patiently." He taps out his pipe on the parapet. "That deacon is greedy. But he is not stupid. And he isn't Zhao Heng's man, not entirely. I watched him look at your Second Uncle's numbers."

"Seventy-two," says Lin Jian.

"Seventy-two," his grandfather agrees.

They sit together on the wall for a long time, looking west, the old man and the boy, and neither of them says anything else.
